wa_mojo_rising.overview: A direct-start variation to the Northwest Face on SEWS, first climbed III 5.11 A1 (with a short section of aid) by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Tom Smith, October 13-14, 2006; the 5.11b grade reflects later free ascents of the aid section.

wa_cutthroat_the_swarm.beta: Eight pitches of varied climbing culminate in four bolted headwall pitches rated 5.10-5.11 (bolted anchors placed on lead for everything above 5.9), with natural gear protecting the lower and upper pitches. Notable pitches include "The Gem" (a splitter finger crack, pitch 3) and a sustained dihedral-jamming crux pitch (pitch 6).
wa_cutthroat_the_swarm.overview: A modern, sustained 5.11 alpine testpiece up Cutthroat's East Face, with four gear-protected headwall pitches (5.10-5.11) on bolted anchors linking natural, less-traveled terrain below and above — a quality alternative to the crowded Liberty Bell group just to the south.

wa_ultramega_ok.descent_text: Ultramega OK has no independent, well-established rappel line of its own — it is a Northeast Buttress route and most parties finish by merging into upper North Face terrain (traversing near Burgundy Ledge) rather than topping out cleanly on a dedicated line. From wherever the route is topped out, the standard way down is the North Face's 5-rappel descent: ~40m from a heavily slung summit boulder down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor; ~55m from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch (traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings); ~55m from that constriction down to a blue-slung horn; ~40m from the horn to broad scree ledges (watch the rope pull here — lots of snag potential); and a final ~60m to the base of the first-pitch chimney, near where Action Potential and the North Face start. Double 60m ropes make this clean; parties with a single 70m have reported getting down with some downclimbing between stances, but it's tighter on this line than on the standard North Face. From the base of the raps, reverse the Burgundy Col approach back to the highway. A few parties describe instead downclimbing loose 3rd/4th-class terrain on Burgundy's east side back toward the col to avoid rappelling altogether, but this is opportunistic route-finding rather than an established descent, and is not recommended in the wet or for parties unfamiliar with the terrain.

wa_king_kong_gorillas_direct_direct.fa: Sol Wertkin & Tyree Johnson, 2016 (freed by Sol Wertkin)

wa_southwest_face.descent_text: From the summit, several parties instead scramble roughly 30 feet north along the summit ridge, descend a short gully/chimney, follow easy slabs down and north to a major gully, work up to a narrow notch in the summit ridge, cross it (a belay is prudent), and continue north to a descent gully leading down the north end of the west face — but for most parties the simplest option is to downclimb the route's own ledge system back to Pineapple Pass and retrace the approach; rappelling the loose east-side gully carries notable rockfall hazard and is not recommended.

wa_dragontail_peak_r3.overview: Pandora's Box (also called the W Couloir) is the standard moderate couloir linking Colchuck and Dragontail near Colchuck Col. It's a west-facing snow/talus couloir a couple hundred feet east of Colchuck Col, most often climbed as the summit finish for Dragontail Peak via the Colchuck Glacier approach. The couloir is class 3 scrambling with sections of steep snow up to roughly 40-45°; it is not a technical ice or mixed climb. A single ice axe, crampons, and comfort on steep snow/talus are the normal kit. The true summit pinnacle itself involves an optional short 5.6 move for parties who want the exact high point.
wa_dragontail_peak_r3.descent_text: From the top of the couloir/Pandora's Box, descend left and traverse northeast to the true summit (some parties rope up for this exposed traverse), or alternatively exit about 30 ft below the notch, scramble Class 4 rock roughly 20 ft, and follow the ridge left to the top. From the summit, the standard descent is southeast to a saddle, then east across a long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, then down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake - stay climbers' left near the granite walls and beware drifting climbers' right into cliffs near Colchuck Peak. Crampons/axe are recommended into mid-summer; early season the descent can largely be glissaded. No rappels are needed on this standard summit-and-Aasgard-Pass finish. If a party instead retreats directly back down the couloir rather than topping out, downclimbing steep snow/ice or building an improvised rappel off natural gear (slung chockstones or horns) in the couloir could become necessary - this specific scenario is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for on a technical, mixed alpine couloir.

wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson/Klickitat glacier basins — a long, mostly-off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Given the route's distance (~27 km) and gain (6,700 ft) roughly match the other long approach routes on this mountain, expect a full day just to reach a camp near the toe of the Wilson Glacier before a summit attempt.
